lessons.title: Field Drying: Sun and Wind Techniques
lessons.body: After cutting your grass, the first job is to get it dry as fast as possible. In most of Africa, the sun is strong, but humidity and unexpected rain can ruin your hay. The goal is to reduce moisture from about 75-80% (fresh grass) down to 15-20% for safe storage. Field drying relies on sun and wind. Cut early in the morning after the dew has dried, so the grass has the whole day to dry. Use a sharp sickle or machete, or a simple mower if you have one. Spread the grass in a thin layer, not clumps. A thin layer exposes more surface to sun and wind. In very hot areas, you might need to dry for only 1-2 days; in cooler or humid areas, 3-5 days. Turn the grass once or twice a day with a wooden rake or pitchfork to expose the underside. If you have a tractor, a hay tedder helps, but manual turning works. Watch the weather: if clouds build up, cover the hay with a tarpaulin or move it under shelter. In windy areas, use windrows (long rows) perpendicular to the wind to speed drying. But don't make rows too thick. Test dryness by twisting a handful: if it breaks easily and no moisture squeezes out, it's close. Aim for 18-20% moisture. If you dry too much (below 15%), leaves shatter and you lose nutrients. If too wet, mould grows. So check daily. In humid regions like coastal West Africa, field drying may take longer; consider adding salt (1-2 kg per 100 kg grass) to help preserve, but that's not traditional hay. Better to dry thoroughly. Remember, hay quality depends on quick drying. The longer it stays wet, the more sugars and vitamins are lost. So start early, spread thin, turn often, and bring in before evening dew if not fully dry.

lessons.title: Tedding and Raking to Speed Up Drying
lessons.body: Tedding and raking are simple actions that can cut drying time by a day or more. Tedding means fluffing up the grass to expose more surface to air and sun. You can do this with a pitchfork or a wooden rake. After the grass has wilted for a few hours, go through the swath and toss it lightly. This is especially important if the grass is thick or if humidity is high. Do it once in the morning and once in the early afternoon. Raking, on the other hand, is gathering the partially dried grass into windrows (long rows) to dry evenly and to prepare for baling. Use a wooden or bamboo rake, or a simple hay rake with curved teeth. Rake when the grass is about 40-50% moisture (still flexible but not dripping). Rake in the late afternoon when dew is not yet falling. Make windrows that are about 1-1.5 meters wide and 30-50 cm high. This allows air to circulate. If you have a tractor, a side-delivery rake or a tedder can do this faster, but manual methods work for small plots. In very sunny areas, you might ted twice a day. In humid areas, tedding is critical to prevent mould. Be careful not to rake too early when grass is too wet, as it can clump and mould. Also, avoid raking when it's too dry, because leaves shatter and you lose the most nutritious parts. The best time to rake is when the grass is like leather: flexible but not brittle. After raking, let the windrows dry for another half day or full day, then test moisture. If you plan to bale, rake into windrows that match your baler or hand-baling method. For hand baling, smaller windrows are easier to handle. Tedding and raking are labour-intensive but low-cost. They are essential for quality hay in African conditions where humidity can be high.

lessons.title: Testing Moisture Content Without a Meter
lessons.body: You don't need an expensive moisture meter to know if your hay is ready to bale or store. Use your senses and simple tests. The most common field test is the twist test: take a handful of hay and twist it tightly. If it feels soft and cool, and no moisture drips out, it's likely around 20-25% moisture. If it feels brittle and breaks when twisted, it's below 15% and may be too dry. For baling, the ideal range is 18-20% moisture. Another test is the salt test: put a pinch of dry salt in a jar with a sample of hay, shake, and if salt sticks to the hay, it's too wet. If it falls off, it's dry enough. You can also use a simple oven method: weigh a small sample (say 100g), dry it in an oven or solar dryer at low heat until constant weight, then reweigh. The weight loss is moisture. For example, if 100g becomes 80g, moisture is 20%. But in the field, use the twist and feel test. Another method: press a handful of hay into a ball. If it springs back and feels dry, it's ready. If it stays in a ball and feels damp, it's too wet. Also, listen: dry hay crackles when you rub it; wet hay is silent. For storing in stacks, you want moisture below 20%. If you store hay at 25% moisture, it will heat up and mould. So test before baling and again before storage. In humid areas, aim for 15-18% moisture. If you're unsure, better to dry an extra day. Remember, over-drying causes leaf loss, so don't go below 15%. Practice these tests on small batches to calibrate your senses. With experience, you'll be able to judge moisture by feel and sound. This skill is crucial for small-scale farmers without meters.

lessons.title: Avoiding Rain Damage and Mould Growth
lessons.body: Rain is the biggest enemy of hay. A single rain shower on nearly dry hay can ruin it. When hay gets wet, moulds and bacteria grow, producing toxins that can harm livestock. So you must protect hay from rain. First, watch the weather. In many African regions, rains come in the afternoon. So plan to cut early, dry fast, and bale before rain. If rain threatens, cover the hay with a tarpaulin, plastic sheet, or even banana leaves. But don't cover it so tightly that it sweats; leave some air circulation. If hay gets wet, spread it out to dry again immediately. If it's already in windrows, turn them to expose wet parts. If mould starts to grow (you'll see white, grey, or black patches, and smell a musty odour), do not feed it to animals, especially pregnant ones. Mouldy hay can cause abortions and illness. To prevent mould, ensure hay is properly dried before storage. Also, store in a dry place. In humid areas, consider adding a natural preservative like salt (1-2% by weight) or molasses, but salt can cause rust in metal equipment. Another method is to make haylage (wrapped silage) but that's different. For hay, the key is moisture below 20%. If you must store hay that is slightly wet, add salt at 1 kg per 100 kg hay to inhibit mould. But better to dry it. Also, avoid storing hay on bare ground; use a raised platform or pallets. In the field, if rain is frequent, consider making smaller batches that dry quickly. Or use a solar dryer or barn. Remember, mouldy hay is dangerous. If you see mould, discard it or use as compost. Never feed mouldy hay to young or pregnant animals. Prevention is better than cure: dry thoroughly, protect from rain, and store dry.

lessons.title: Baling Hay by Hand or with Simple Presses
lessons.body: Baling makes hay easier to handle, store, and transport. You can bale by hand or with a simple press. For hand baling, you need twine (sisal or plastic) and a frame. A simple frame can be made from wooden poles: two uprights and a crossbar. You place hay in a rectangular box (about 50x40x40 cm) and compress it by standing on it or using a lever. Then tie the bale with twine in a figure-eight pattern. A typical small bale weighs 15-25 kg. To make it, layer hay in the box, compress, add more, and tie when full. For a simple press, you can use a car jack or a lever system to compress hay into a box. The goal is to make dense bales that shed water and take less space. In Africa, many farmers use a manual baler made from a 200-litre drum cut open, with a plunger. You fill the drum with hay, compress with the plunger, and tie. Bale size can vary. For hand baling, wear gloves to avoid cuts. Use twine that is strong; two strings per bale are enough for small bales. If you have a tractor, a round baler is faster, but for small-scale, hand baling is fine. Baling should be done when hay is at 18-20% moisture. If too dry, leaves shatter; if too wet, mould. After baling, leave bales in the field to dry a bit more if needed, but protect from rain. Stack bales in a dry place. Baling reduces storage space by half compared to loose hay. It also makes feeding easier. You can sell bales. So learn to bale by hand; it's a skill that adds value. Start with small bales and practice. With a simple press, you can make 20-30 bales a day with two people.

lessons.title: Storing Hay in Stacks and Lofts
lessons.body: Proper storage protects hay from rain, ground moisture, and pests. The two main methods are stacks (outdoor or indoor) and lofts (above animal housing). For stacks, choose a well-drained site. Put a layer of stones, branches, or pallets on the ground to keep hay off the soil. Build the stack with the driest hay in the center and slightly wetter hay on the outside? No, all hay should be dry. Make a stack that is wider at the base and tapers to the top, like a pyramid, so rain runs off. Cover with a thatched roof, tarpaulin, or plastic sheet. In humid areas, indoor stacks are better. A simple hay barn with a roof and open sides allows air circulation. For lofts, store hay above animal pens. The animals' body heat rises and keeps the hay dry. But ensure the loft is well-ventilated and not leaking. Before storing, test moisture again; it should be below 20%. If you store hay at 25% moisture, it will heat up and could even catch fire. So never store wet hay. In the stack, put a few sticks or bamboo poles vertically to allow air movement. Check the stack regularly for heating: put your hand inside; if it's warm, it's fermenting. If hot, dismantle and dry. Also, watch for mould. For long-term storage, keep hay in a dry, dark place. In Africa, many farmers store hay in a corner of the house or in a separate hut. Make sure it's off the ground and covered. If you have no shelter, a well-built stack with a good thatch can last through the dry season. But rain can still penetrate, so check after storms. Hay stored properly can last 6-12 months. So invest in a simple storage structure. It will save your feed and money.

quiz.q: What is the ideal moisture content for baling hay?
quiz.explanation: Hay should be baled at 18-20% moisture to avoid mould while preventing leaf shattering.

quiz.q: Which test can you use to check if hay is dry enough without a meter?
quiz.explanation: Both the twist test and salt test are simple field methods to estimate moisture.

quiz.q: What is tedding?
options: B) Fluffing up hay to expose it to air
D) Covering hay with a tarp
quiz.explanation: Tedding means fluffing up the hay to increase exposure to sun and wind for faster drying.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid raking hay when it is too dry?
options: B) Leaves shatter and nutrients are lost
quiz.explanation: When hay is too dry, the leaves become brittle and shatter, leading to loss of the most nutritious parts.

quiz.q: What is the main risk of storing hay with high moisture?
options: C) It heats up and moulds
quiz.explanation: High moisture hay can heat up, mould, and even spontaneously combust.

quiz.q: In field drying, why should you spread grass in a thin layer?
options: A) To make it easier to collect
B) To expose more surface to sun and wind
C) To prevent it from blowing away
quiz.explanation: A thin layer allows better air circulation and sun exposure, speeding up drying.

quiz.q: What is a windrow?
options: B) A long row of hay
quiz.explanation: A windrow is a long, narrow row of hay left to dry in the field.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign that hay is too wet for storage?
options: B) It feels cool and damp
C) It breaks easily when twisted
D) It is light in colour
quiz.explanation: If hay feels cool and damp, it still has too much moisture and is not ready for storage.

quiz.q: What should you do if hay gets rained on?
options: A) Leave it to dry in the sun
C) Cover it with a tarp and leave it
D) Spread it out to dry again
quiz.explanation: If hay gets wet, spread it out to dry again to prevent mould growth.

quiz.q: What is a simple method to compress hay for baling by hand?
quiz.explanation: A car jack can be used as a simple press to compress hay into a bale.

quiz.q: Why is it important to store hay off the ground?
options: A) To prevent it from blowing away
C) To avoid ground moisture and pests
D) To make it easier to count
quiz.explanation: Storing hay off the ground prevents moisture absorption and reduces pest damage.

quiz.q: What is the recommended moisture content for storing hay in stacks?
quiz.explanation: Hay should be below 20% moisture for safe storage to prevent mould and heating.

quiz.q: What is a loft in hay storage?
options: B) A storage area above animal housing
quiz.explanation: A loft is an upper level in a barn or above animal pens used for storing hay.

quiz.q: What does the salt test for hay moisture involve?
options: A) Mixing salt with hay and seeing if it sticks
C) Adding salt to hay before baling
D) Using salt to dry hay
quiz.explanation: In the salt test, if salt sticks to the hay, it indicates the hay is still too wet.

quiz.q: Which factor is most important for rapid field drying?
quiz.explanation: Sun and wind are the primary drivers of field drying for hay.

quiz.q: What is the ideal time of day to cut grass for hay?
quiz.explanation: Cutting after dew has dried allows the grass to dry faster during the day.

quiz.q: What happens if you store hay at 25% moisture?
options: B) It heats up and moulds
quiz.explanation: At 25% moisture, hay is too wet and will heat up and grow mould.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of raking hay?
options: B) To gather it into windrows
quiz.explanation: Raking gathers hay into windrows for even drying and later baling.

quiz.q: What is a simple sign that hay is dry enough for baling?
options: A) It feels cool and damp
quiz.explanation: Dry hay crackles when rubbed, indicating low moisture.

quiz.q: Why is mouldy hay dangerous?
options: B) It can cause illness and abortions in animals
D) It is hard to bale
quiz.explanation: Mouldy hay contains toxins that can cause illness, especially in pregnant animals.

quiz.q: What is a hay stack?
options: B) A pile of hay built for storage
quiz.explanation: A hay stack is a large pile of hay built for storage, often covered.

quiz.q: How can you prevent rain damage to hay in the field?
quiz.explanation: Covering hay with a tarpaulin protects it from rain.

quiz.q: What is the twist test for hay?
options: A) Twisting a handful to see if moisture drips
quiz.explanation: The twist test involves twisting a handful of hay to check for moisture release and flexibility.

quiz.q: What is the recommended bale weight for hand baling?
quiz.explanation: Hand bales typically weigh 15-25 kg for easy handling.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid over-drying hay?
options: B) Leaves shatter and nutrients are lost
quiz.explanation: Over-drying makes leaves brittle, causing them to shatter and lose nutrients.

quiz.q: What is a simple storage structure for hay?
options: B) A barn with open sides
quiz.explanation: A barn with open sides allows air circulation while protecting from rain.

quiz.q: What does it mean if hay feels warm in the stack?
options: B) It is fermenting and may mould
C) It is ready to feed
quiz.explanation: Warm hay indicates microbial activity and potential mould growth.

quiz.q: What is the benefit of tedding hay?
quiz.explanation: Tedding fluffs up hay, increasing exposure to sun and wind, thus speeding drying.

quiz.q: Which tool is commonly used for raking hay by hand?
quiz.explanation: A wooden rake is a simple tool for gathering hay into windrows.

quiz.q: What is the main advantage of baling hay?
options: B) It reduces storage space and eases handling
quiz.explanation: Baling compresses hay, reducing storage space and making it easier to handle and transport.
